example.answer: The curve crosses the y-axis at y = −3, passes through (10, 97), and is a parabola opening upwards.
example.problem: Plot y = x^2 − 3 from x = −10 to x = 10.
steps: Type x^2 - 3 in the function box — the ^ sign means 'to the power of'.
Set x min to −10 and x max to 10 to frame the view.
The graph draws a U-shaped parabola. At x = 0, y = 0² − 3 = −3, so the curve crosses the y-axis at −3.
At x = 10, y = 100 − 3 = 97, showing how fast a square grows.
example.title: Graphing y = x² − 3

faqs.a: Type ^ for powers (x^2), * for multiplication, and / for division. Functions are written as words: sin(x), cos(x), tan(x), sqrt(x), abs(x), ln(x) and log(x). Constants pi and e are available too.
faqs.q: How do I type powers and functions?

faqs.a: Only the whitelisted characters are accepted, and the expression is compiled in strict mode with no access to anything outside x and the Math functions. It cannot read or change anything on the page.
faqs.q: Is it safe to type anything into the function box?

faqs.a: It means the function is undefined there: 1/x at x = 0, or sqrt(x) for negative x. The calculator breaks the curve at those points instead of joining across the gap, so you see the true shape.
faqs.q: Why does the curve break or have gaps?

faqs.a: Change x min and x max to zoom. A smaller window like −2 to 2 zooms in on detail near the origin; a bigger window shows the overall shape. The y range rescales automatically to fit what is visible.
faqs.q: How do I zoom in on part of the graph?

howItWorks: You type a function of x in plain text, for example x^2 - 3 or sin(x). Before anything runs, the expression is checked against a strict whitelist: only x, numbers, the operators + − * / ^, brackets, a comma, and the words sin cos tan sqrt abs ln log pi e may appear. Anything else is rejected with a clear message.

The safe expression is then translated for the browser: ^ becomes the power operator, sin becomes Math.sin, ln becomes the natural log, log becomes the base-10 log, and pi and e become their numeric constants. The result is compiled into a function of x that can read nothing else, so typing in the box cannot harm the page.

To draw the graph, the calculator samples 400 points evenly across your x range and finds the smallest and largest y values to set the vertical scale automatically. It draws a grid with labelled ticks, bolder axes through the origin when they are in view, and then plots the curve in red — lifting the pen wherever the function is undefined, so gaps like 1/x at x = 0 show correctly. The readouts below the graph give the exact y value at x = 0 and at both ends of your window.
intro: Type any function of x — like x^2 - 3, sin(x) or 1/x — and watch it drawn instantly on a labelled grid with axes. Set your own x window, and get exact values at x = 0 and at both ends of the range.

mistakes.text: Writing x2 means x times 2, not x squared — always include the * sign: 2*x. Likewise 3(x+1) needs a sign: 3*(x+1). The parser reads exactly what you type.
mistakes.title: Forgetting the multiplication sign

mistakes.text: sin x without brackets is rejected; write sin(x). Brackets also fix order of operations: 1/x+1 is (1/x)+1, while 1/(x+1) is a different function — bracket what you mean.
mistakes.title: Skipping brackets around functions

mistakes.text: Trig functions here use radians, matching most graphing tools and programming languages. sin(pi/2) = 1, but sin(90) is about 0.894. Use the pi constant to write radian angles.
mistakes.title: Expecting degrees in trig functions

mistakes.text: x^2^3 is parsed as x^(2^3) = x^8, because ^ groups to the right. If you meant (x^2)^3 = x^6, add the brackets.
mistakes.title: Stacking powers without brackets
